info.text: Visual analysis asks how a painting's elements and composition guide attention, and how its historical setting shapes what those choices may mean.

clusters.name: Visual elements
clusters.fact: Line, color, light and shadow, and texture are basic visual resources through which a painting creates form, mood, emphasis, and surface.

line.text: An actual or implied path that can define edges, suggest movement, divide space, or direct the viewer's eye.

color.text: Hue, value, and intensity used to distinguish forms, create contrasts, establish mood, or carry associations.

light and shadow.text: Variations in brightness that model form, create depth, establish atmosphere, or emphasize selected areas.

texture.text: The actual or depicted surface quality of a work, such as smoothness, roughness, thickness, or visible brushwork.

clusters.name: Composition
clusters.fact: Composition organizes a painting's parts through focal points, balance, scale, and perspective, shaping the order in which viewers notice and relate them.

focal point.text: The area designed to attract attention first or most strongly within the composition.

balance.text: The distribution of visual weight across a composition, whether symmetrical, asymmetrical, or deliberately unstable.

scale.text: The relative size of figures, objects, and spaces, which can suggest depth, importance, intimacy, or monumentality.

perspective.text: A system for representing spatial depth and viewpoint on a flat surface.

clusters.name: Historical setting
clusters.fact: A painting's subject, intended audience, original location, and historical moment help explain why it was made and how its first viewers may have understood it.

subject.text: The person, event, story, place, or idea represented in the painting.

intended audience.text: The viewers for whom the work was made or displayed, whose expectations can shape its form and message.

original location.text: The architectural, devotional, civic, domestic, or commercial setting for which the painting was first made or displayed.

historical moment.text: The political, religious, economic, and cultural conditions present when the work was produced.

bridges.fact: Visual hierarchy uses contrasts in color, light, line, size, and placement to direct attention and establish an order of importance within the composition.

info.text: The perceived order of importance created when some visual elements stand out more strongly than others.

bridges.fact: Iconography interprets depicted subjects, attributes, gestures, and symbols by comparing visible details with the cultural traditions and historical setting that made them meaningful.

info.text: The identification and interpretation of subjects, symbols, and conventional details in images.

bridges.fact: Patronage can shape a painting's scale, format, subject, audience, and original location because commissioners often influence what is made and where it will be seen.

info.text: Support or commissioning provided by a person or institution that enables and may influence the production of art.
